_model: A meal is one idea that can be obtained three ways. Each route is independently nullable and independently reviewed, because they arrive at different times and are different judgements: whether a delivery plan suits a GLP-1 appetite, whether a shelf-stable product is a sensible choice, and whether a recipe's arithmetic is right. A meal ships as soon as any one route is reviewed.

_routes.delivered: A subscription service ships it cooked. Highest protein, highest commission, needs an approved affiliate programme. null until one approves.
_routes.prepared: Shelf-stable products from Amazon. Label nutrition, real ASINs, fits the existing multi-item cart.
_routes.made: A recipe. Highest protein per pound, no commission beyond pantry items, gated on dietitian review.

_macros: carbs, fat and fiber are null until they come from a label or a sourced composition value. They are never estimated to fill the field -- a null renders as nothing, an invented number renders as a fact.
_prepared: kind distinguishes what the products in this route are. 'substitutes' is a list of alternatives -- pick one -- carried over from the old buy[] list, and its route protein is null because summing alternatives would invent a number nobody could eat. 'entree' is a single prepared meal that stands in for the whole dish, and it carries real label nutrition. All four migrated meals are 'substitutes'; sourcing their entree twins is the next piece of work.
_preferences: Preference is the hard problem here, and it is not the usual one. On a GLP-1, aversions move week to week -- meat aversion and metallic taste are characteristic, and cooking smells set off nausea. A one-time 'set your dietary preferences' onboarding, which is what every other meal planner does, is the wrong shape for this audience. The question is 'what can you not face today', asked every time, so a meal has to be tagged on the axes people actually reject on rather than the axes a recipe site indexes by.
_vocabularyNote: temperature and aroma are single values; the rest are lists. Every value must appear in _vocabulary -- a typo'd tag silently stops matching and the meal quietly disappears from every plan, which is the same class of fault as a mistyped ingredient losing its affiliate link. A test enforces it. These are first-pass judgements and exactly the kind of thing the dietitian should correct, being a use of her time that checking arithmetic is not.
_unlinkedNote: Ingredients we deliberately do not link. Nobody needs an affiliate link for a lemon. Anything unlinked and NOT listed here fails tests/dishes.test.js, which is how a typo like 'Chicken breast' gets caught before it silently loses its link.

dishes.title: Seared salmon with lemony chickpeas
dishes.blurb: A whole meal in one pan, and one of the easier things to face when appetite is low — the lemon cuts the richness that puts people off fish on a bad day.

products.name: Premier Protein Shake
products.note: when even this is too much cooking

steps: Warm the oil in a pan over a medium heat. Season the salmon and lay it in skin-side down.
Leave it four to five minutes without touching it, then turn and give it two more.
Lift the salmon out. Tip the chickpeas into the same pan with a squeeze of lemon and warm through.
Stir the spinach in until it just wilts, then put the salmon back on top.
made.tip: On a nauseous day, serve it cold from the fridge the next morning. Cold fish is often easier than hot, and it loses nothing.

dishes.title: Cold protein bowl, no cooking
dishes.blurb: For the mornings when the thought of cooking is worse than the thought of eating. Nothing here needs heat, and it takes about two minutes.

products.name: Fairlife Core Power
products.note: the same idea in a bottle

products.name: Whey Protein Powder
products.note: stir a scoop through the yogurt

steps: Spoon the yogurt into a bowl.
Scatter the berries over — straight from frozen is fine, they thaw as you eat.
Add the almonds and chia and leave it a minute if you like it thicker.
made.tip: Make it the night before. Half the battle on a bad morning is that nothing is ready.

dishes.title: Chicken and lentil traybake
dishes.blurb: The highest-protein thing on this site for the least attention. Everything goes in one tin and the oven does the rest.

products.name: Quest Protein Bar
products.note: for the days cooking is not happening

ingredients.name: Lentils
ingredients.qty: 100 g cooked, or half a tin

steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Toss the vegetables with the oil in a roasting tin.
Sit the chicken on top, season, and give it 20 minutes.
Stir the lentils in around the chicken and return it for 5 minutes to warm through.
Check the chicken is cooked through before serving.
made.tip: Cook two and keep one cold. A cooked chicken breast in the fridge is the difference between hitting your protein and giving up on it.

dishes.title: Cottage cheese scramble
dishes.blurb: Stirring cottage cheese through eggs adds protein without adding volume, which matters when a full plate is the problem.

products.name: Egg Whites
products.qty: swap one egg for a splash

steps: Beat the eggs and season them.
Cook gently, stirring, and take the pan off the heat while they still look slightly underdone.
Fold the cottage cheese and spinach through — the residual heat finishes both.
made.tip: Low and slow. Rushed scrambled eggs go rubbery, and rubbery eggs are very hard to eat on a bad day.

dishes.title: Tuna and white beans, straight from the tin
dishes.blurb: Nothing is heated and nothing is cooked. A tin, a pouch and a bag of spinach, which is about the limit of what is possible on a bad day.

steps: Tip the beans into a sieve and rinse them under the cold tap.
Put the spinach in a bowl, the beans on top, then flake the tuna over with a fork.
Trickle the oil over and squeeze on some lemon if you have it.
made.tip: Rinsing the beans is worth the thirty seconds -- it takes most of the tinned taste away, which matters more than usual when your sense of taste has changed.

dishes.title: Cold prawns with edamame and avocado
dishes.blurb: Bought ready-cooked, assembled in a bowl. No heat, no smell, and a lot of protein for something that takes four minutes.

ingredients.name: Cooked prawns
ingredients.qty: a small pack, cooked and peeled

steps: Run the edamame under the cold tap to thaw them, or leave them out for ten minutes.
Tip everything into a bowl and slice the avocado over the top.
made.tip: Frozen edamame thaw in a sieve under cold water in about a minute, which is the only reason this is a four-minute meal rather than a twenty-minute one.

dishes.title: Chickpeas and boiled eggs with cucumber
dishes.blurb: Boil the eggs whenever you feel well and keep them in the fridge. Then this is assembly, not cooking.

steps: Rinse the chickpeas and tip them onto a plate.
Halve the eggs and set them on top with the cucumber.
Splash the oil over, and plenty of black pepper.
made.tip: Boil six eggs at once on a good day. Cold hard-boiled eggs keep about a week and turn several bad days into a two-minute meal.

dishes.title: Smoked salmon over cold lentils
dishes.blurb: The most protein here for the least effort, and the lentils bring the fibre that most cold meals do not.

steps: Tip the lentils onto a plate straight from the pouch.
Drape the salmon over and tuck the cucumber in around it.
Splash the oil over and add a squeeze of lemon.
made.tip: Smoked salmon is salty, which is often welcome when nothing tastes of much -- but it is the saltiest thing on this site, so it is not an everyday meal.

_nutrition: Meals added from September 2026 derive their figures rather than stating them. Each ingredient names a pinned USDA FoodData Central id and a weight in grams (ops/data/ingredients.json), and ops/nutrition.py sums them. The id is pinned, not searched at build time, so a search returning a different food next month cannot silently change a published number. The first four dishes still carry hand-worked figures and should be converted.
